quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'The' plus an '-est' adjective signals the extreme end of a scale.
quests.explanation: Subject (This) + verb (is) + superlative (the busiest) + noun (day) + 'of the year'. Superlatives use 'the' and compare one thing against an entire group.
quests.textToSpeak: This is the busiest day of the year.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Tallest' picks him out from everyone else on the team.
quests.explanation: Subject (He) + verb (is) + superlative (the tallest) + noun (player) + 'on the team'. The superlative singles out one member from a larger group.
quests.textToSpeak: He is the tallest player on the team.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: Longer adjectives use 'most' instead of an '-est' ending.
quests.explanation: Subject (That) + verb (was) + superlative (the most expensive) + noun (mistake) + clause (we made). Multi-syllable adjectives form superlatives with 'most', not '-est'.
quests.textToSpeak: That was the most expensive mistake we made.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Might' expresses uncertainty — weaker than 'will', stronger than a guess.
quests.explanation: Subject (It) + 'might' + base verb (rain) + time (later this afternoon). 'Might' shows the speaker isn't sure something will happen.
quests.textToSpeak: It might rain later this afternoon.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Could' here guesses a reason, not describing past ability.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + 'could be' + adjective (stuck) + 'in traffic'. 'Could' can express a present possibility, not only past ability.
quests.textToSpeak: She could be stuck in traffic.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: The negative slips between 'might' and the verb, then 'until' marks the earliest likely time.
quests.explanation: Subject (They) + 'might not' + base verb (answer) + 'until Monday'. 'Until' shows the point before which the action probably won't happen.
quests.textToSpeak: They might not answer until Monday.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Someone' stands for an unknown person, acting as the subject.
quests.explanation: Subject (Someone) + verb (left) + object (a bag) + place (near the entrance). Indefinite pronouns like 'someone' work exactly like a regular subject noun.
quests.textToSpeak: Someone left a bag near the entrance.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Anyone' appears here because the sentence is negative — not 'someone'.
quests.explanation: Subject (I) + 'didn't tell' + object (anyone) + topic (about the surprise). Negative sentences typically use 'anyone', while positive ones use 'someone'.
quests.textToSpeak: I didn't tell anyone about the surprise.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Nothing' itself carries the negative meaning — no separate 'not' is needed.
quests.explanation: Subject (Nothing) + verb (seems) + 'to work' + place (on this printer). 'Nothing' already means 'not anything', so the verb stays positive in form.
quests.textToSpeak: Nothing seems to work on this printer.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Himself' shows the action loops back to the same person who did it.
quests.explanation: Subject (He) + verb (taught) + reflexive pronoun (himself) + 'how to code'. Reflexive pronouns show the subject and the object are the same person.
quests.textToSpeak: He taught himself how to code.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Ourselves' matches the plural subject 'we' — both refer to the same group.
quests.explanation: Subject (We) + verb (blamed) + reflexive pronoun (ourselves) + 'for the delay'. 'Ourselves' must agree with a plural subject like 'we'.
quests.textToSpeak: We blamed ourselves for the delay.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Herself' follows the verb directly, before the phrase naming who she met.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + verb (introduced) + reflexive pronoun (herself) + 'to the new team'. 'Introduce oneself' is a common fixed expression with a reflexive pronoun.
quests.textToSpeak: She introduced herself to the new team.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Used to' signals a habit or state that isn't true anymore.
quests.explanation: Subject (I) + 'used to' + base verb (live) + place (in a small town). 'Used to' describes a repeated past state that has since changed.
quests.textToSpeak: I used to live in a small town.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: In the negative, 'used' loses its 'd' — listen closely for that small change.
quests.explanation: Subject (They) + 'didn't use to' + base verb (argue) + degree (this much). 'Used to' drops the 'd' after 'didn't', becoming just 'use to'.
quests.textToSpeak: They didn't use to argue this much.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: The question form matches the negative — 'used' becomes 'use' here too.
quests.explanation: 'Did' + subject (you) + 'use to' + base verb (play) + object (an instrument)? Questions with 'used to' also drop the 'd', just like negatives do.
quests.textToSpeak: Did you use to play an instrument?

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'How long' asks about duration, and 'does' follows for this routine question.
quests.explanation: 'How long' + 'does' + subject (the flight) + frequency (usually) + base verb (take)? 'How long' asks about the amount of time something requires.
quests.textToSpeak: How long does the flight usually take?

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'How far' asks about distance, paired simply with 'is' since there's no action verb.
quests.explanation: 'How far' + verb (is) + subject (the hotel) + 'from here'? 'How far' measures distance rather than time or frequency.
quests.textToSpeak: How far is the hotel from here?

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'How often' asks about frequency, and 'do' follows for this habitual question.
quests.explanation: 'How often' + 'do' + subject (you) + base verb (update) + object (the website)? 'How often' questions ask about the rate or frequency of an action.
quests.textToSpeak: How often do you update the website?

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'So' builds up the adjective, and 'that' introduces the consequence it caused.
quests.explanation: Subject (The line) + verb (was) + 'so' + adjective (long) + 'that' + result (we left). 'So...that' links a strong quality to its direct result.
quests.textToSpeak: The line was so long that we left.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: The result clause explains exactly what happened because of the quiet speaking.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + verb (spoke) + 'so' + adverb (quietly) + 'that' + result (nobody heard). 'So' can intensify an adverb, not only an adjective.
quests.textToSpeak: She spoke so quietly that nobody heard.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: The cause comes first, and the surprising effect follows 'that'.
quests.explanation: Subject (It) + verb (got) + 'so' + adjective (cold) + 'that' + result (the pipes froze). 'So...that' often introduces an extreme or surprising outcome.
quests.textToSpeak: It got so cold that the pipes froze.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Too heavy' means more than can be managed, and 'to carry' shows the blocked action.
quests.explanation: Subject (The box) + verb (was) + 'too' + adjective (heavy) + 'to' + verb (carry) + 'alone'. 'Too...to' shows a quality that prevents an action.
quests.textToSpeak: The box was too heavy to carry alone.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Enough' follows the adverb here, then 'to get' shows what became possible.
quests.explanation: Subject (He) + verb (arrived) + adverb (early) + 'enough' + 'to' + verb (get) + object (a seat). 'Enough' after an adverb shows a sufficient degree that allows an action.
quests.textToSpeak: He arrived early enough to get a seat.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Too small' blocks easy reading, explained by the 'to' phrase that follows.
quests.explanation: Subject (This font) + verb (is) + 'too' + adjective (small) + 'to' + verb (read) + manner (easily). 'Too...to' shows a quality strong enough to prevent an outcome.
quests.textToSpeak: This font is too small to read easily.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Pick up' is a two-word verb acting as a single unit meaning 'buy' or 'collect'.
quests.explanation: 'Can' + subject (you) + phrasal verb (pick up) + object (some milk) + time (later)? 'Pick up' here means to buy something while out.
quests.textToSpeak: Can you pick up some milk later?

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Looking for' means searching, and the object follows directly after 'for'.
quests.explanation: 'We're' (We are) + phrasal verb (looking for) + object (a bigger apartment). 'Look for' is a fixed phrasal verb meaning to search for something.
quests.textToSpeak: We're looking for a bigger apartment.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Give up' means quitting, and 'on' introduces what shouldn't be abandoned.
quests.explanation: 'Don't' + phrasal verb (give up) + 'on the project' + 'yet'. 'Give up on' means to stop trying with something or someone.
quests.textToSpeak: Don't give up on the project yet.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: A superlative leads, then 'so' connects it to the response that followed.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (This was the hardest exam I took) + 'so' + clause 2 (I studied all weekend). A superlative can justify an action described afterward with 'so'.
quests.textToSpeak: This was the hardest exam I took, so I studied all weekend.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: A past habit is directly contrasted with the present, joined by 'but' and 'now'.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (I used to dislike mornings) + 'but' + clause 2 (now I actually enjoy them). 'Used to' plus a present-tense contrast is a natural way to describe change over time.
quests.textToSpeak: I used to dislike mornings, but now I actually enjoy them.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Too long' explains the problem, and 'so' introduces the decision made because of it.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (The queue was too long) + 'so' + clause 2 (we came back later instead). 'Too' plus an adjective can justify a decision explained afterward with 'so'.
quests.textToSpeak: The queue was too long, so we came back later instead.
